channel.title: OT/ICS Threat Intel - Oil & Gas
channel.description: Curated OT/ICS advisories, incidents and threat intelligence. Editorial by Mike Holcomb in partnership with UtilSec.

item.title: [Critical] Coast Guard and FBI cyber teams boarded two US-bound energy tankers after signs their networks had been compromised — no disruption, and no confirmed cause yet
item.category: Top Story
item.description: Reporting on 16 September disclosed that US Coast Guard and FBI cyber teams boarded two foreign-flagged tankers bound for the United States in late August. The first boarding, on 21 August, was the very large crude carrier VL Prosperity, owned by GMF GLV No. 4 SA and managed by HMM Ocean Service; the second followed on 24 August. Accounts differ on the second vessel — Rigzone, carrying Bloomberg reporting, describes an unidentified LNG carrier, while ABC News describes both ships as oil tankers. US authorities say the boardings were to check the integrity of the vessels’ operational and IT systems “following indications that the vessel’s network were compromised by foreign cyber actors.” VL Prosperity had lost communications for about 30 hours in the Strait of Gibraltar after loading crude at Sidi Kerir, Egypt, an outage Iran’s Mehr News Agency was first to call a cyberattack. Authorities reported no operational disruption, no loss of vessel stability, no danger to crew and no environmental impact, and VL Prosperity was cleared to resume normal operations. Neither the cause nor any attribution has been confirmed; ABC reports investigators are examining whether Iran or another actor was responsible. For oil and gas operators this is the seaborne end of the supply chain showing up in a federal cyber response — and a reminder that terminal-to-ship interfaces are part of the attack surface. - ABC News reporting on the US Coast Guard and FBI boardings, corroborated by Rigzone carrying Bloomberg reporting; cause and attribution unconfirmed, and the two outlets differ on the second vessel’s type - Boardings 21 and 24 Aug 2026; first reported 16 Sep 2026

item.title: [Medium] CenterPoint Energy confirms customer data was taken through an external-facing system — gas and electric delivery not affected
item.category: Incident — Customer data theft at a gas and electric utility; no OT impact
item.description: CenterPoint Energy, the Houston-based electric and natural gas utility, said in an SEC filing that an unauthorised third party obtained personal information on “a portion of the Company’s customers through one of the Company’s external-facing systems.” BleepingComputer reports the system was a public API with no rate limiting, web application firewall or automated access controls. Exposed data includes names, phone numbers, service and billing addresses, account numbers, billing amounts and partial Social Security numbers. An actor using the alias “4d722e4d656f77” claims to have taken 7.49 million records and has leaked data; CenterPoint has not given a count, and class-action filings allege the intrusion ran from 17 August to 1 September. The company says electric and natural gas services were not affected, and it has notified law enforcement and regulators. This is an IT and customer-data incident, not an OT one, and it is scored that way. It belongs on an oil and gas page because gas distribution utilities run exactly this kind of customer-facing API alongside SCADA for pressure and flow — and the useful question is how much those two estates share. - CenterPoint Energy SEC filing, reported by BleepingComputer and The Record; record count claimed by the actor, not confirmed by the company - Intrusion alleged 17 Aug–1 Sep 2026; company disclosure and reporting 15 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] The US puts up to $10 million on the IRGC cyber commander said to direct CyberAv3ngers — energy is on the named target list
item.category: Threat Intelligence — Nation-state actor behind PLC attacks, US reward offer
item.description: On 4 September the US State Department’s Rewards for Justice programme offered up to $10 million for information on Amir Yaryab, described as a senior official of Iran’s IRGC Cyber-Electronic Command (IRGC-CEC) who leads its Cyber Operations Command. The State Department says he directs IRGC-CEC components and affiliated groups including CyberAv3ngers, Dadeh Afzar Arman and Mehrsam Andisheh Saz Nik, and that these groups have targeted critical infrastructure in the United States, Europe and the Middle East, energy and telecommunications among them. Analysis published by Security Boulevard on 9 September also names the Shahid Hemmat and Shahid Shushtari components, and ties Iran-linked groups to attacks on municipal water systems in at least 12 US states this year. The technical background is the joint CISA and FBI warning updated on 22–23 July, which said Iran-affiliated actors attacking PLCs in water and energy had widened their target set beyond Rockwell/Allen-Bradley to Schneider Modicon M340/BMX P34 and Siemens S7-1200 controllers. Those are the controller families found in wellsite automation, compressor stations, tank farms and terminal loading systems. The reward is a policy step, not a new intrusion, and the attributions are US government assessments. - US State Department Rewards for Justice announcement, reported by RFE/RL via GlobalSecurity and analysed by Security Boulevard; technical background from the CISA/FBI update reported by Cybersecurity Dive - Reward announced 4 Sep 2026; analysis 9 Sep 2026; joint advisory updated 22–23 Jul 2026

item.title: [High] Red Heron broke into self-hosted Gitea and walked out with SCADA and HMI source code from an industrial automation vendor
item.category: Threat Intelligence — PRC-linked campaign, SCADA/HMI source code theft
item.description: Acronis’ Threat Research Unit published findings on 13 September, reported on 14–15 September, on a campaign it attributes with moderate confidence to Red Heron, a Chinese-speaking, PRC-linked actor, exploiting CVE-2026-60004, the CVSS 9.8 Gitea remote code execution flaw fixed in Gitea 1.27.1 on 27 July. Acronis and Industrial Cyber count at least 11 compromised organisations across Canada, Argentina, Taiwan, the United States and Sri Lanka (The Hacker News reports 13 in six countries), including a Canadian renewable energy company, a Taiwanese industrial automation firm, municipal platforms and defence, aerospace and telecoms organisations. From the automation firm the attackers took the source code of a SCADA/HMI tool used in industrial control environments, along with IoT integrations and a network sniffer; “hundreds of repositories” were exfiltrated from a single target. The tooling includes the JITTERLY implant, a previously undocumented Linux rootkit Acronis calls SIXZUT, and the Adaptix C2 framework. No oil or gas victim has been reported. The relevance is twofold: stolen HMI source gives an attacker a head start on finding flaws in products that end up in process plants, and O&G engineering teams and integrators increasingly keep PLC logic, HMI projects and SIS configuration in exactly this kind of self-hosted Git server. - Acronis Threat Research Unit research, reported by Industrial Cyber; victims unnamed, attribution moderate confidence - Acronis research 13 Sep 2026; reporting 14–15 Sep 2026; Gitea flaw in KEV since 25 Aug 2026

item.title: [High] The NCSC says OT targeting is up across multiple sectors globally and has already caused real-world disruption — and that you should not assume your OT is unreachable
item.category: Threat Intelligence — National agency alert on OT targeting
item.description: The UK National Cyber Security Centre published a formal alert on 27 August stating it has seen increased targeting of operational technology across multiple sectors globally, including in the UK, by a range of threat actors, and that the activity has resulted in some limited real-world disruption. It names no victims, actors or techniques. The part worth reading in an oil and gas control room is the framing: organisations should not assume their OT is unreachable from the internet without verifying it, because exposure arises through misconfiguration, legacy connections and unmanaged assets. That describes the dispersed upstream and midstream estate almost exactly — wellpads, remote valve and meter stations, compressor sites and offshore telemetry commissioned by a contractor, connected over cellular or satellite, and rarely re-surveyed afterwards. The alert sets out eight actions covering internet exposure, credentials, boundary-device support, controller modes, logging and restoration. - UK National Cyber Security Centre alert, “Disruptive cyber activity highlights risk from internet-exposed systems and edge devices” - Published 27 Aug 2026

item.title: [Medium] August set a global ransomware record at 997 attacks — energy incidents so far are landing on IT, and that is where the outage comes from
item.category: Threat Intelligence & Research — Ransomware statistics
item.description: Comparitech data reported on 14 September recorded 997 ransomware attacks worldwide in August 2026 — about 32 a day, a 23 percent rise on July’s 809 and above the previous monthly record of 988 in February 2025. Attacks on businesses reached 861 and on healthcare 69, while attacks on utilities doubled from five to ten. Qilin, with 157 claims, and The Gentlemen, with 107, together accounted for more than a quarter of the total. Treat the absolute numbers with caution: counts of this kind rest largely on leak-site claims and disclosure practice, and a claimed victim is not a confirmed one. The data does not break out oil and gas. The pattern it fits is nonetheless the one the sector already knows from Colonial Pipeline onward — encryption lands on business systems, and operations stop because scheduling, billing, custody-transfer accounting or terminal ticketing depends on them, not because anything touched a controller. - Comparitech monthly ransomware tracking, reported by Industrial Cyber; counts largely based on actor claims and do not break out oil and gas - Data for August 2026; reporting published 14 Sep 2026

item.title: [Info] Six steps to being able to disconnect — and a planning horizon of three months running isolated
item.category: Research — Isolation readiness, practitioner guidance
item.description: Nozomi Networks published a practitioner summary on 2 September of the Five Eyes “CI Fortify” guidance released on 28 July, reducing it to six steps: identify vital systems and their dependencies; establish trust levels and connection maps; pre-build the separation points; create and test graduated isolation plans; retain visibility while isolated; and run post-isolation checks before reconnecting. The step that changes the engineering is keeping monitoring alive after the link is cut, because an isolation plan that also blinds the control room will not be executed under pressure. The addition worth arguing about is the planning horizon: Nozomi suggests operators assume they may need to sustain isolated operations for up to three months. For a pipeline or a refinery that pushes the question beyond network design into leak-detection models that pull data from enterprise systems, licence servers, time synchronisation, and how long a DCS can run without its business-network dependencies. - Nozomi Networks Labs analysis of the CISA / ASD ACSC / NCSC-UK / CCCS “CI Fortify” guidance - Analysis published 2 Sep 2026; underlying guidance published 28 Jul 2026

item.title: [High] A hard-coded key and MD5 password hashes inside AVEVA Pipeline Integrity Monitor — read access to the project files is enough
item.category: Critical Advisory — Pipeline leak detection and integrity monitoring
item.description: CISA published advisory ICSA-26-253-01 on 10 September covering four vulnerabilities in the PIMBoards component of AVEVA Pipeline Integrity Monitor, AVEVA’s real-time leak-detection and integrity product for liquid and gas pipelines. All versions up to and including 2025 SP1 P1 are affected. CVE-2026-81821, a hard-coded cryptographic key (CVSS v3 8.4), lets anyone who can read PIMBoards project files decrypt the sensitive information inside them. CVE-2026-81822, weak MD5 password hashing (CVSS v3 8.4), exposes password hashes to brute force and a potential route to administrator access. CVE-2026-81823, missing authorisation (5.3), allows unauthorised reads of PIMBoards data, and CVE-2026-81824, a cross-site scripting flaw (4.7), lets a malicious link run script in a user’s session. AVEVA found the first two itself; researcher Adham Khairy Ramadan reported the others. The fix is the 2025 SP1 P2 security update, and AVEVA notes that migrating legacy project files to the new cryptography is one-way. No exploitation has been reported. This is the most directly pipeline-specific advisory of the period: whoever can read or administer PIM can see, and potentially change, the leak-detection configuration and dashboards that controllers rely on for safety decisions. - CISA ICS advisory ICSA-26-253-01 and AVEVA security bulletin, reported by ISSSource and SecurityWeek - Advisory published 10 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] Schneider fixes a CVSS 9.2 authentication flaw in Modicon M580 and M580 Safety — and SCADAPack RTUs are in the same release
item.category: Critical Advisory — Process and safety controller authentication
item.description: Schneider Electric’s September Patch Tuesday release on 8 September included SEVD-2026-251-04 for CVE-2026-3869, an incorrect implementation of an authentication algorithm (CWE-303) scored CVSS v4.0 9.2. The weakness is exposed when a project built at a lower application level runs, and can affect confidentiality, integrity and availability. Affected are Modicon M580 at application levels below 4.00 and Modicon M580 Safety below 4.20; Blastwave’s analysis says Modicon MC80 is also affected. The same release fixed a medium-severity defect in SCADAPack x70 RTUs and a high-severity issue in PowerLogic T300, and updated four existing advisories. Nothing in the release is reported as exploited. The sector relevance is our assessment rather than the vendor’s: M580 and M580 Safety controllers run process and safety functions in gas processing, terminals and refinery units, and SCADAPack RTUs are a common choice for wellsite automation and pipeline telemetry. An authentication weakness in a safety-rated controller is the kind of finding that belongs in the SIS change process, not the general patch queue. - Schneider Electric security notice SEVD-2026-251-04, with analysis from Blastwave and the September Patch Tuesday round-up in SecurityWeek; oil and gas applicability is editorial assessment - Released 8 Sep 2026 (September ICS Patch Tuesday)

item.title: [Critical] A Sandworm-linked cluster and a Qilin ransomware operator got into Cisco firewall management consoles — the consoles that set your IT/OT boundary rules
item.category: Critical Advisory — Exploited firewall management platform, CISA KEV
item.description: Cisco and CISA confirmed on 9 September that CVE-2026-20079 in Cisco Secure Firewall Management Center is being exploited in the wild. It is a CVSS 10.0 authentication bypass: a remote, unauthenticated attacker sends crafted HTTP requests and gains root on the appliance. CISA added it to KEV the same day with a federal remediation deadline of 12 September, now passed. Cisco Talos describes three post-compromise clusters. UAT-12197 used CVE-2026-20079 and is not attributed to a named actor. UAT-11823, an APT whose tooling overlaps with the Russian group Sandworm, used CVE-2026-20079 together with CVE-2026-20316 and deployed a variant of Cyclops Blink — Talos does not say Sandworm itself was responsible. UAT-11988, assessed as a ransomware operator, got in only through CVE-2026-20316, a static-credential flaw, and ultimately deployed Qilin. No OT impact and no oil and gas victim has been named. But FMC is where the firewall policy between corporate networks and plant, pipeline SCADA and terminal control networks is written, so root on FMC is the ability to quietly loosen that boundary. - Cisco security advisory update and Cisco Talos research of 9 Sep 2026, plus the CISA KEV addition — reported by SecurityWeek, cluster detail corroborated by The Hacker News - Advisory updated and KEV listing added 9 Sep 2026; reporting 10 Sep 2026; federal deadline 12 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] A CVSS 10 pre-auth flaw in SonicWall’s SMA1000 remote-access gateway is being exploited — and CISA says patching alone does not close it
item.category: Critical Advisory — Actively exploited remote-access gateway, KEV-listed
item.description: SonicWall disclosed on 1 September that two previously unknown vulnerabilities in its SMA1000 secure remote access gateway are being exploited in the wild. CVE-2026-83548, scored CVSS 10, is a pre-authentication server-side request forgery in the Appliance Work Place interface; CVE-2026-83549, at 7.8, is an operating-system command injection flaw in the Appliance Management Console. Chained, they give an unauthenticated attacker remote code execution on the appliance. CISA added both to KEV on 2 September with a 5 September federal deadline and flagged both for forensic triage under Binding Operational Directive 26-04 — a signal that patching does not end the incident. Affected models are the SMA1000 6210, 7210 and 8200v; SSL-VPN on SonicWall firewalls and the SMA 100 series are not affected. Remote-access gateways like this are how automation vendors, integrators and on-call engineers reach DCS, SCADA and terminal systems out of hours, which makes the appliance a boundary device whether or not it is inventoried as one. - SonicWall PSIRT advisory and CISA KEV addition of 2 Sep 2026 — reported by BleepingComputer, corroborated by SecurityWeek and Help Net Security - Vendor advisory 1 Sep 2026; added to CISA KEV 2 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] CISA’s 8 September KEV batch is led by a CVSS 10 pre-auth flaw in the RMM platform your managed-service provider may use
item.category: Critical Advisory — Actively exploited RMM platform, KEV-listed
item.description: CISA added four vulnerabilities to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 8 September, all with vendor fixes available. The one that matters most for oil and gas operations is CVE-2026-86218 in N-able N-central, scored CVSS 10.0: a static code injection weakness giving pre-authentication remote code execution on the remote monitoring and management server. N-able has confirmed exploitation in the wild, Huntress reported attacks against N-central’s API from 4 September, and N-able shipped 2026.3 Hotfix 4 on 5 September — its fourth hotfix in five weeks. The federal deadline of 11 September has passed. RMM agents run with high privilege on the hosts they manage, and at smaller producers, midstream gathering operators and fuel distributors, IT is frequently outsourced to an MSP whose agents sit on the same Windows servers that host historians, SCADA clients or terminal automation. The batch also carries two exploited Windows privilege-escalation zero-days, CVE-2026-81963 in the Update Stack and CVE-2026-85880 in ALPC, both giving SYSTEM, plus an Adobe Commerce template-injection flaw. - CISA KEV catalog addition of 8 Sep 2026 — corroborated by BleepingComputer, SecurityWeek and CyberScoop reporting on the N-able and Microsoft disclosures - Added to KEV 8 Sep 2026; N-able hotfix released 5 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] CISA adds five exploited flaws to KEV, including ScreenConnect — the remote-support tool that turns up on vendor-supplied OT PCs
item.category: Critical Advisory — Confirmed exploited remote-support and build tooling
item.description: CISA added five vulnerabilities affecting JFrog Artifactory, ConnectWise ScreenConnect and MikroTik RouterOS to the KEV catalog on 12 September on evidence of active exploitation, with federal remediation deadlines of 13 September for RouterOS, 14 September for ScreenConnect and 25 September for Artifactory. Reporting indicates the Artifactory flaws were chained to gain administrator control, establish persistence and install Rust-based backdoors; ScreenConnect exploitation reportedly enabled unauthorised file transfer and execution through active sessions using a malicious VBScript payload; and the RouterOS entry reflects the CERT Polska chain covered separately on this page. No oil and gas victim is named. The ScreenConnect entry is the one to read twice: remote-support tools are how OEM service desks and integrators reach compressor-control panels, analyser shelters, terminal automation PCs and engineering workstations, and they are often installed by the vendor rather than by the operator’s own security team. - CISA KEV catalog addition — reported by The Hacker News - KEV addition 12 Sep 2026; reporting 13 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] “MikroTrick” is now confirmed exploited — two CVSS 9.2 SSH flaws hand over RouterOS admin on the routers at remote sites
item.category: Critical Advisory — Confirmed exploited, remote-site edge routers
item.description: CERT Polska issued an alert on 9 September confirming that the MikroTik RouterOS chain known as “MikroTrick”, disclosed earlier but not previously confirmed as exploited, is being used in real-world attacks observed since at least 2 September. The chain pairs an SSH authentication bypass, CVE-2026-67276 at CVSS 9.2, with an SSH privilege-escalation flaw, CVE-2026-86060 at CVSS 9.2, to take full unauthenticated administrative control of an internet-exposed RouterOS device. A third bug, CVE-2026-67277, allows memory disclosure or denial of service through the bandwidth-test service. CISA added the exploited flaws to KEV on 12 September. CERT Polska named no victims or sectors, only that MikroTik devices are widely deployed by ISPs, enterprises and critical-infrastructure networks, so there is no confirmed oil and gas victim. It earns its place here because inexpensive, capable routers are a common contractor choice for cellular and fixed-wireless backhaul at wellpads, tank batteries, remote valve and meter stations — often the one device on site with a route to both the SCADA host and the internet. - CERT Polska alert — reported by Industrial Cyber; CISA KEV addition 12 Sep 2026. No victims or sectors named - Exploitation observed from 2 Sep 2026; CERT Polska confirmation 9 Sep 2026; KEV listing 12 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] Dutch NCSC warns exploitation of two CVSS 9.8 Check Point VPN flaws is imminent — patches landed 9 September
item.category: Critical Advisory — VPN gateway, exploitation assessed imminent
item.description: The Netherlands’ National Cyber Security Centre issued a warning, reported on 12 September, that it expects near-term exploitation of two critical vulnerabilities in Check Point VPN products, CVE-2026-85102 and CVE-2026-85103, both carrying CVSS 9.8 in reporting. The pair can allow unauthenticated remote code execution on Security Gateways, and a certificate-decoding defect can also affect Security Management Servers. Check Point released fixes on 9 September. No public proof-of-concept had been reported and no exploitation confirmed at the time of the warning — the NCSC’s position is a forecast, not an observation. Firewall and VPN gateways of this class commonly sit at the IT/OT boundary of refineries, gas plants and pipeline control centres, where they often terminate the vendor and contractor tunnels into those networks. - Dutch National Cyber Security Centre warning — reported by BleepingComputer; exploitation assessed as imminent, not confirmed - Check Point fixes 9 Sep 2026; NCSC warning reported 12 Sep 2026

item.title: [Medium] September ICS Patch Tuesday: Siemens ships nine advisories and starts fixing the “Copy Fail” Linux kernel flaw across its product lines
item.category: Critical Advisory — September ICS Patch Tuesday round-up
item.description: Siemens published nine new advisories and updated nine existing ones in the 8 September ICS patch round. The critical-severity findings are in the Reyrolle 7SR5 relay family, Open Interface Services, Industrial Edge Management and SIMOVE Fleetmanager/SIPLANT; Desigo CC, Teamcenter, the Mendix SAML module and Element Maps received high-severity fixes. Siemens also began shipping updates across affected products for the Linux kernel “Copy Fail” vulnerability, CVE-2026-31431 at CVSS 7.8, which can give a local attacker a root shell. In the same cycle Schneider Electric fixed the Modicon M580 authentication flaw covered separately above, and AVEVA published the Pipeline Integrity Monitor advisory also covered above, while noting a previously disclosed medium-severity deserialisation issue in AVEVA Enterprise SCADA. Nothing in the round is reported as exploited. Most of Siemens’ items are grid, building or edge products rather than oil and gas specific, but Industrial Edge and embedded Linux devices appear in upstream and refinery digitalisation projects, and AVEVA Enterprise SCADA is widely used for pipeline control. - Siemens ProductCERT, Schneider Electric and AVEVA security advisories of 8 Sep 2026 — summarised by SecurityWeek - Advisories published 8 Sep 2026

item.title: [Medium] Rockwell patches more than a dozen flaws in early September — RSLinx Classic, Logix controllers and the 1756-ENBT module among them
item.category: Critical Advisory — Vendor patches, Logix controllers and communications
item.description: CISA published eight ICS advisories on 1 September, five of them Rockwell Automation, and SecurityWeek’s round-up on 2 September counted more than a dozen Rockwell vulnerabilities across products. ICSA-26-244-01 covers four denial-of-service flaws in RSLinx Classic 4.50 and earlier — CVE-2026-9621, -9622, -9624 and -9625 — each triggerable remotely with a single crafted Common Industrial Protocol packet and no authentication, fixed in 4.60. Other advisories reach the Logix platform, including ControlLogix 5580, CompactLogix 5380, GuardLogix 5580 and Compact GuardLogix 5380, the Redundancy Module Configuration Tool and FactoryTalk Activation Manager. SecurityWeek also reports a denial-of-service issue in the 1756-ENBT communications module, published by CISA as ICSA-26-246-05, and a high-severity remote code execution flaw in FactoryTalk Historian. One controller flaw, CVE-2026-9637, was initially described as exploited; that was corrected, and CISA confirmed no known exploitation. ControlLogix and CompactLogix chassis with 1756-ENBT modules are common in compressor stations, gas processing, loading racks and wellsite automation, where a controller or communications crash can trip or stall the process. - CISA ICS advisories ICSA-26-244-01 through -05 (1 Sep 2026) and ICSA-26-246-05, with the Rockwell round-up reported by SecurityWeek - Advisories published 1–3 Sep 2026; round-up reported 2 Sep 2026

item.title: [Medium] The Coast Guard now has one office that owns maritime cyber policy — relevant to every waterfront oil and LNG terminal it regulates
item.category: Regulation — US Coast Guard maritime cyber governance
item.description: The US Coast Guard has established the Office of Maritime Cybersecurity Policy (CG-MCP) under its Director of Inspections and Compliance, as the central authority for cybersecurity policy across the Marine Transportation System. Its remit is to develop domestic policy, contribute to international standards, direct a unified compliance and enforcement strategy, and serve as the main point of contact for industry. The move follows Government Accountability Office findings on gaps in Coast Guard cyber oversight, including weak incident tracking and missing personnel competency standards. Nothing in the maritime cyber rule changes today. The relevance to oil and gas is that the Coast Guard is the security regulator for waterfront facilities handling crude, refined products and LNG, and it was Coast Guard cyber teams, with the FBI, that boarded the US-bound tankers in the top story. Consolidating policy and compliance under one office usually means the same questions, asked the same way, at more facilities. - US Coast Guard announcement — reported by SecurityWeek and Industrial Cyber - Office establishment reported 1 Sep 2026

item.title: [Info] Six agencies publish outage-communication guidance — the standard your shippers, customers and regulators will hold you to
item.category: Policy — Joint international guidance, incident communications
item.description: On 2 September the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security joined CISA, Australia’s ASD ACSC, NCSC-NZ, NCSC-UK and the FBI to publish joint guidance on communicating during IT and OT service outages, “Communicating Under Pressure: Best Practices for Service Providers.” It asks providers to hold a written incident communications plan with defined trigger thresholds and named audiences, send plain-language updates rather than legal boilerplate, give affected users root-cause and technical detail they can act on, and align messaging with legal and regulatory duties. Pipeline and terminal operators are service providers in exactly this sense. The 2021 Colonial Pipeline shutdown showed how quickly an unexplained halt becomes a fuel-supply and public-confidence problem when shippers, retailers and the public are left to fill the gap themselves. - CISA and the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security — joint guidance “Communicating Under Pressure: Best Practices for Service Providers” - Published 2 Sep 2026

item.title: [Info] 117 federal reporting rules across 27 agencies — and the first hours of a pipeline incident are when they collide
item.category: Policy — Federal incident reporting
item.description: The McCrary Institute and the US Chamber of Commerce published analysis on 8 September, drawing on Government Accountability Office work, counting 117 separate federal cyber incident reporting regulations spread across 27 agencies, 48 of which apply to private industry. Their argument is operational: duplicative notifications with different thresholds, formats and clocks pull the same small group of people away from containment during the hours when containment matters most. Oil and gas operators will recognise the shape. A single cyber event can touch TSA’s pipeline security directive reporting to CISA, Coast Guard reporting for marine terminals, SEC disclosure for listed companies, state regulators, cyber insurers and contractual notice to shippers and customers. The analysis lands as the CIRCIA rules are expected to be finalised this autumn, which is when harmonisation either happens or does not. - McCrary Institute and US Chamber of Commerce analysis citing GAO data, reported by Industrial Cyber - Published 8 Sep 2026; CIRCIA final rule expected autumn 2026
